newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO to talk, East Jerusalem plan slowed.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO to talk, East Jerusalem plan slowed.

text.p: Israel on Monday put the brakes on a plan to build a new Jewish enclave in Arab East Jerusalem and agreed to resume talks with the PLO on meeting commitments made under their interim peace deals.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) praised the moves as steps to restore confidence but stressed a months-long deadlock on proceeding with final peace talks continued.

Israel's Interior Ministry suspended a permit granted to a U.S. Jewish land baron to build 70 Jewish homes in Ras al-Amoud Arab neighbourhood until an appeal by two left-wing Jerusalem city council members against the plan had been heard.
Palestinians, who want East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state, have said the project would bury Middle East peace moves.
Suspension of the plan, though technical, bought time for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu -- who had said he would work to block it in an effort to try to defuse the latest crisis.

Israel's Channel Two Television meanwhile said Netanyahu, who said he first heard of the permits for the Ras al-Amoud project on Thursday after the Jerusalem municipality approved them, had been briefed on the plan two days before by Israel's Interior Minister Eliahu Suissa.
Suissa in a statement to the media confirmed he met Netanyahu on Tuesday and briefed him on a wide range of issues, from local elections to the pending Ras al-Amoud project.
"The prime minister directed on that issue that the delay in plans continue," Suissa said, backing Netanyahu's claim that the granting of the permit two days later took him by surprise.
Israeli-PLO peace talks have been in crisis since March when Israel broke ground on the 6,500-home Har Homa settlement on an East Jerusalem hill known to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Saeb Erekat, the PLO's senior negotiator, earlier accused Netanyahu of using the Ras al-Amoud project to appear "dovish" to the world and divert attention from the larger settlement.
"If settlement activities continue, there really would be no peace process. Any peace intiative has to include a halt to settlement activities," Erekat told Reuters.
But Palestinians were pleased the Ras al-Amoud plan had been stopped for now.
"We feel that stopping the action there contributes to the confidence that is being built," PLO negotiator Nabil Shaath said after talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Monday.
Levy and Shaath agreed that joint Israeli-PLO committees would renew talks on outstanding issues from a 1995 peace deal.
They include the opening of Gaza air and sea ports, a "safe passage" for Palestinians between the West Bank and Gaza Strip and the release of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel.
Levy said Israel agreed to the move after receiving assurances from Palestinian President Yasser Arafat that he would cooperate with Israel in "the war on terror".

Shaath said the resumption of committees signalled "the desire to go the second phase" but said: "The issues upon which this deadlock developed still await solution: the issues of settlement, Jerusalem, and the return to (final) negotiations".

Palestinians demand a halt to settlement activity as the price to restart peace talks. Israel, which annexed East Jerusalem after capturing it in 1967, says it can build where it likes in the city it calls its united capital.
Netanyahu fended off right-wing Israeli criticism of his intention to block the latest Jerusalem building plan.

"What is first and foremost important to understand that we want to build in Jerusalem and we will continue to build in Jerusalem...(Ras al-Amoud) is not the right place and it's not the right time," Netanyahu told Israel Television.
Netanyahu has said work will continue at Har Homa.
The Jerusalem District Appeal Committee will hold a hearing on the challenge to the Ras al-Amoud project on August 5.
